                        REQUEST FOR REHEARING AND CLARIFICATION
                        OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC

           Pursuant to Section 313 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) 1 and Rule 713 of the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 2 Constellation

Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) respectfully requests that the Commission grant

rehearing and clarification of its September 29, 2026, Order Accepting Reliability Backstop

Procurement and Establishing Further Procedures. 3

           BACKGROUND

           On July 31, 2026, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) submitted revisions to the PJM

Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among

Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”). 4

Numerous parties filed comments and protests addressing the proposal, including Constellation.5

            REQUEST FOR REHEARING AND CLARIFICATION

           A.       The Commission Erred in Rejecting Constellation’s Proposed Eligibility
                    Revisions for RBP Resources and Resources Eligible to Supply Qualifying
                    RBP Offset UCAP MW

           Constellation requested 12 that the Commission require PJM to modify the criteria set forth

in the RBP Proposal so that resources like Eddystone could qualify as RBP Resources or as

resources eligible to provide Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW. Specifically, Constellation

recommended that PJM modify the criteria listed in Sections 18.2 and 18.5 of the proposed Tariff

to clarify that Energy Resources (i.e., energy-only resources with no capacity rights) seeking new

CIRs through an Interconnection Request would be eligible to supply Qualifying RBP Offset

UCAP MW and qualify as an RBP Resource. 13

           As currently drafted, Section 18.5 of the proposed Tariff requires a generation or Energy

Storage Resource offered as an RBP Resource to meet certain criteria, including that such RBP

Resources be:

                    (i)    Composed of new Installed Capacity and new Maximum Facility
                    Output;

                    (ii)   Supported by new Capacity Interconnection Rights (if located in the
                    PJM Region) or Capacity Interconnection Rights transferred from a
                    deactivated resource or a resource that announced deactivation as of April
                    10, 2026; and

                    (iii) Consist of (1) new build; (2) incremental capacity created by an
                    uprate of an existing Generation Capacity Resource’s or Energy Storage
                    Resource’s installed capacity and associated level of Capacity
                    Interconnection Rights; or (3) repowering of a generation resource that had
                    deactivated, or announced deactivation, on or before April 10, 2026. 14

            B.         The Commission Did Not Justify Mandatory Price-Taker Treatment

                      1.    The Commission Failed to Engage in a Reasoned Balancing Analysis

           In its Order, the Commission rejected the arguments of Constellation and other commenters

objecting to the RBP Proposal’s price taker requirement, stating that “the Commission has

consistently found that Regional Transmission Organizations and Independent System Operators

can reasonably require resources that are compensated outside of the capacity market because they

are needed to maintain reliability to offer as price-takers in capacity auctions to avoid double

procurement, even at the risk of price suppression.” 26

           Notably, as support for its finding, the Commission cited to its RMR precedent, without

providing any additional analysis. The Order’s reliance on RMR precedent does not supply the

missing analysis. 27 Unlike in the RMR proceedings, in the Order the Commission failed to engage

in a reasoned balancing analysis to determine whether it is just and reasonable in these

circumstances to require out-of-market resources to offer as price takers. Any such meaningful

analysis would find that on balance the facts presented here, unlike in the RMR proceedings, weigh

in favor of finding that the RBP Proposal’s price taker requirement is unjust and unreasonable

given the material and potentially long-lived effect it may have on RPM price formation for years

to come.

             RMR arrangements generally retain existing units for limited periods to address identified

transmission-reliability violations affecting existing load. 28 The RBP instead may place 6,831.3

MW of forecast-driven, separately compensated capacity into repeated RPM Auctions as price-

taker supply for as long as fifteen years, even though the associated load may energize later than

forecast (or not at all).

            Those distinctions concern the very factors the Commission has considered when balancing

the reliability rationale for out-of-market support against its effect on market price formation and

the potential impacts on resource adequacy in the long-term: purpose, magnitude, duration, and

certainty of need. Yet paragraph 53 simply concluded that the RBP is “likewise” entitled to price-

taker treatment because both RBP and RMR resources are procured outside RPM for reliability

purposes. Characterizing the arrangements at that level of generality does not explain why their

material differences are irrelevant, or why, in this instance, the price-taker requirement is just and

reasonable.

            Further emphasizing the Commission’s failure to engage in any meaningful and reasoned

balancing analysis here is the Commission’s precedent in ISO New England, in which the

Commission engaged in an extensive analysis weighing the potential effects of out-of-market

resources. 29       There, the Commission found that self-supplied resources participating in the

capacity auction as price-takers could have a price suppressing effect on the market. The

Commission explained that “just and reasonable market rules must achieve” the objective of

“preventing [out-of-market] resources from distorting the market clearing price.” 30 Ultimately,

 and after “weighing all the interests and evidence before it,” the Commission found that “the

appropriate course of action, which result in just and reasonable rates, is to prevent new resources

from lowering the price of capacity significantly below competitive levels” by, in that case,

            In ISO New England, the Commission was so concerned with the price suppressive effect

from price-taker bidding in the capacity auction and the potential to “inhibit competitive

investment” that it mandated offer floor mitigation. 32 Here, the Order performs no comparable

balancing analysis of the RBP’s scale, duration, timing mismatch, or effect on entry and retention

signals.

                    2.    The Order Did Not Address the Matched Isolation Mechanism,
                          Which Was Supported by Expert Testimony

            PJM justified mandatory price-taker treatment as necessary to prevent RPM from procuring

capacity already secured through the RBP. Paragraph 53 accepted that rationale without adequately

considering the countervailing market and long-term resource adequacy impacts of such approach

or addressing the mechanism Constellation proposed.

            PJM suggested that RBP resources must be offered into RPM as a price-taker to ensure

load does not “double pay” for capacity. But as Constellation explained in previous filings, the

price-taker requirement will undermine RPM as a credible price-forming market and resource

adequacy will be hindered. A mandatory $0/MW-day offer is not just or reasonable, and does more

harm than good, because it will signal excess supply if anticipated load is delayed or does not show




31
     Id.

32
     Id. at P 70.


                                                   13
 up. 33 The resulting signal can reduce retention and entry incentives, accelerate resource exit, and

defer new investment in the region. Such a result recreates the very resource adequacy problems

that spurred the RBP in the first place.

            As Constellation explained in its Limited Protest, these results can be avoided, and load

can still be protected from the double payment, if instead PJM isolates the RBP supply and

corresponding RBP-related demand from the RPM. By utilizing the isolation method instead of a

price-taker requirement, the market will not result in distorted RPM prices that signal excess

supply and encourage retirement of the existing fleet if anticipated load is delayed. 34

            Constellation did not propose removing RBP supply while leaving the full associated

demand requirement in RPM. For each applicable auction, Constellation’s proposed mechanism

would exclude Available RBP UCAP from the price-forming supply stack and reduce the

applicable reliability requirement by the lesser of Available RBP UCAP and RBP-Related Load

reflected in that auction’s Planning Parameters. The mechanism therefore prevents duplicate

procurement for the matched quantity by adjusting both supply and demand, while avoiding the

one-sided price-forming effect of mandatory zero offers.

            Paragraph 53 of the Order claimed that the price-taker requirement was necessary, despite

“the risk of price suppression,” in order to avoid double procurement. 35 But the Order ignored Dr.

Shanker’s supporting analysis and Constellation’s recommended proposal to isolate RBP supply

and corresponding load from RPM price formation, which would have the effect of avoiding both

the risk of double procurement and the risk of distorting RPM prices and the resource adequacy

 consequences that could bring. 36 The Commission therefore acted arbitrarily and capriciously

because it failed to explain why the price taker proposal is just and reasonable in order to avoid

double procurement when the isolation methodology supported by Constellation’s expert witness

will similarly avoid double procurement while also preserving the RPM’s effectiveness for price

formation in support of long-term resource adequacy. 37

            Finally, the Commission recently directed PJM to explain how it would transition back to

“traditional market structures” and avoid “a long-term bifurcation of loads in the PJM market.”38

Although the IRAS Order addressed load treatment, the same concern counsels against embedding

a separate, fifteen-year class of zero-priced RBP supply in RPM. Constellation’s isolation

mechanism would limit, rather than institutionalize, that bifurcation. The Commission’s stated

desire to return to traditional market structures, as noted in the IRAS Order, is at odds with its

acceptance of an RBP proposal that will embed out-of-market distortions in RPM auctions for the

next 15 years. 39

            Given the foregoing, the Commission should grant rehearing and condition acceptance on

the annual isolation mechanism. At minimum, it should reconsider the issue under the correct

record and provide a reasoned response to the matched supply-and-demand adjustment, the ISO-

                   2.      Scope of the Transmission Owner Exit Rules Paper Hearing

          In its Order, the Commission found that the proposed RBP Transmission Owner exit rules

may be unjust and unreasonable, and set the issue for paper hearing.                  Constellation seeks

clarification that the Order neither established a presumption that LSEs in an exiting Transmission

Owner’s zone must bear RBP exit charges nor predetermined the allocation of such charges. To

the extent the Order intended otherwise, the Commission acted arbitrarily and capriciously and

rehearing is warranted.

          The fact that an LSE may have benefited from the original RBP procurement does not

establish that it caused every incremental cost arising from a Transmission Owner’s later

withdrawal. The Transmission Owner controls the withdrawal decision; the affected LSEs

generally cannot prevent, predict, or hedge that event. An exiting Transmission Owner should bear

its appropriate cost burden of generation and load investments made under the assumption that the

Transmission Owner would remain in PJM. 46 At minimum, costs attributable to the withdrawal

decision should not be shifted automatically to LSEs merely because those LSEs benefited from

In addition, the paper hearing should distinguish ordinary RBP Charges attributable to load that

           In its Order, the Commission noted that it has previously found that it is just and reasonable

to impose generation capacity costs on LSEs located within an exiting Transmission Owner’s zone,

separate Transmission Owner’s exit. Constellation therefore requests clarification that the paper

hearing remains open to all allocation approaches and that any replacement rate must separately

identify the relevant cost, cause, and beneficiary. To the extent paragraph 181 intended to prejudge

LSE responsibility, rehearing is warranted.
